content: 1. Poor balance in older adults is strongly associated with an increased risk of falls, disability, and mortality. To address this issue, a systematic review and meta-analysis were conducted to evaluate the effects of free-living physical activity on balance in healthy community-dwelling adults aged 50 years and older. 2. The review included studies from databases such as CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, and others, covering research up to June 7, 2016. Both interventional and observational studies were considered, focusing on the impact of free-living physical activity on balance outcomes. 3. A total of 30 studies met the inclusion criteria. Data extraction and risk of bias assessments were independently performed by two reviewers. Due to the heterogeneity of outcome measures, balance outcomes from observational studies were pooled using standardized mean differences or mean differences with 95% confidence intervals. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) were synthesized using a best-evidence approach. 4. The results indicated that free-living physical activity, ranging from one to 21 years in duration, improved balance measures in older healthy adults. Observational studies showed significant benefits in neuromuscular measures (e.g., gait speed), functionality (e.g., Timed Up and Go, Single Leg Stance, Activities of Balance Confidence Scale), flexibility (e.g., forward reach test), and strength (e.g., isometric knee extension test, ultrasound). 5. A significant effect was also observed in less active groups for a single sensory measure of balance, the knee joint repositioning test. However, the evidence from RCTs was limited and of moderate methodological quality. 6. The review concluded that free-living physical activity has some evidence of effectiveness in improving balance outcomes in older adults. However, future research should focus on higher-quality studies with standardized and clinically relevant balance measures, as well as long-term effects of physical activity on balance. 7. Another systematic review assessed the effects of exercise interventions on preventing falls in community-dwelling older adults. It included 108 RCTs with 23,407 participants, with an average age of 76 years, 77% of whom were women. The primary outcome was the rate of falls. 8. The findings demonstrated that exercises targeting balance, gait, and muscle strength effectively reduced falls in older adults. However, most trials had unclear or high risk of bias, and further research is needed to confirm these results. 9. Yoga has been recommended as a muscle-strengthening and balance activity in physical activity guidelines. A systematic review and meta-analysis of 22 RCTs evaluated the effects of yoga on physical function and health-related quality of life (HRQoL) in older adults without specific clinical conditions. 10. The results showed that yoga interventions significantly improved physical function and HRQoL compared to both active and inactive controls. This evidence supports the inclusion of yoga in physical activity guidelines for older adults as a multimodal activity that enhances strength, balance, flexibility, and mental well-being. 11. Active video games (AVGs) were systematically reviewed to determine their effects on physical performance in older adults. Eighteen RCTs with 765 participants were included, most of whom were healthy community-dwelling older adults. AVGs were found to improve mobility and balance when used alone or as part of an exercise program. 12. However, the suitability of AVGs for older adults with significant cognitive impairments or mobility limitations remains unclear. Further development of age-appropriate AVGs is recommended to address these populations. 13. Physical activity was also explored as a potential strategy to reduce loneliness in adults aged 50 years and older in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs). Data from the Study on Global Ageing and Adult Health (SAGE) revealed that individuals not meeting physical activity guidelines had higher prevalence of loneliness, although this association varied by country. 14. The findings suggest that physical inactivity and loneliness often co-occur in older adults in LMICs. Longitudinal studies are needed to confirm these associations and identify mechanisms to inform future interventions.
